China Announces New Tariffs on Automotive Imports, Impacting Industry Leaders

GUANGZHOU, June 21—A new round of tariffs on imported automotive components took effect across China this week, sending ripples through the country’s auto industry and raising concerns among manufacturers and suppliers. The Ministry of Commerce announced a 25 percent tariff on select categories of electric vehicle (EV) batteries and advanced auto parts, a move aimed at “safeguarding national industry and promoting domestic innovation,” according to a statement released Tuesday.

Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd (CATL), one of China’s premier battery producers, is among the companies currently navigating the shifting landscape. The measure, which applies to certain battery cells and electronic modules sourced from overseas, has prompted immediate adjustments in procurement strategies and production timelines.

“We are assessing supply chain impacts and working closely with our partners to minimize disruption,” a CATL spokesperson told reporters Thursday. “Our commitment to delivering high-quality products to automakers remains unchanged.”

Industry analysts expect the tariffs to push up costs for manufacturers reliant on imported high-performance parts, particularly for electric and hybrid vehicles. “These tariffs are likely to increase the average cost of producing an EV in China by three to five percent in the short term,” said Feng Qiang, chief analyst at the Guangdong Automotive Association. “Firms may need to accelerate local sourcing or negotiate with domestic suppliers to offset the impact.”

The announcement has already caused volatility in local supply chains, with some factories in Guangzhou and Chongqing reporting delays in receiving key electronic components. “We have shipments stuck at customs, and it’s unclear how long the new clearance procedures will take,” said Zhao Li, procurement manager at Dongfang Motors, a mid-sized auto manufacturer.

The China Auto Parts Trade Union expressed concern over potential job impacts if the situation persists. “While we support measures that foster local industry, abrupt policy shifts can create uncertainty for workers and suppliers,” said union representative Wang Yumei.

The government has not specified how long the tariffs will remain in place, stating only that the measure will be “reviewed periodically in light of market developments.” For now, automakers and suppliers are bracing for continued turbulence as they adapt to the evolving trade environment. The full impact of the tariffs remains to be seen as companies like Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd and others adjust to the new regulatory landscape.
